title: Ballroom Blitz
author: Seyward Darby
content:
The White House ballroom project is wildly unpopular. Donald Trump doesn’t care. Ben Terris reports on Trump’s obsessive bid for architectural immortality, which is now barreling toward completion, and captures the breathtaking sycophancy required to work for this president:

“We had asphalt going into here,” Trump says, standing on the pathway leading to the residence of the White House. “Now you have the best stone.” He points at a pile of square-cut granite—the type being used to replace the asphalt walkway—and looks to his communications director, Steven Cheung, who is accompanying us on this impromptu tour of the White House grounds en route to the construction site.

“That’s some stone, huh, Steven?” he says.

“It’s incredible,” Cheung concurs.

“Look at the thickness of it,” Trump says. “Normally, you use one inch, as thin as you can. It’s the White House—I said, ‘Fuck it, what’s the best you have?’ They said, ‘We have one that’s four inches.’”

“You’re restoring glory to the White House,” Cheung says, shaking his head in apparent awe.

I Went to the White House Brawl and Watched the Manosphere Go Limp

Jon Ronson | GQ | August 24, 2026 | 4,492 words

“It was supposed to be an exhibition of freedom without restraint: a bombastic birthday boy, fourteen uncontrollable athletes, and a South Lawn build-out that was piss-your-pants patriotic. But what united onlookers, in the end, was the sudden realization that American machismo had hit a hard limit.”

The Secret History of Trump’s Private Cellphone

title: The Netflix Show That Airs from the Great Beyond
author: @NewYorker
content:
On Wednesday, the feminist pioneer Gloria Steinem died, at ninety-two. The news broke on Thursday morning. By 5 P.M. Eastern time, Netflix had dropped a new episode of “Famous Last Words,” a fascinating series that offers celebrity postcards from the beyond. Each episode features a sit-down interview with a notable person, filmed months or years prior, with the understanding that it will not be released until after the subject’s death. Steinem’s was the third to appear; a conversation with Jane Goodall popped up within forty-eight hours of her death, last October; and another, with the TV heartthrob Eric Dane, came out right after he died, of complications from A.L.S., in February. Not even the show’s producers know the release schedule—that’s up to the chief content officer in the sky.

“My hope is that we’re changing the conversation around fame and around death,” Brad Falchuk, the show’s host and executive producer, told me in May. We spoke again this week, in the hours between Steinem’s death and the appearance of her interview. Falchuk is known as the co-creator, with Ryan Murphy, of such shows as “Glee,” “American Horror Story,” and “Pose.” He’s also famously married to Gwyneth Paltrow. Each episode of “Famous Last Words” begins with his voice-over: “Imagine if we had the opportunity to hear from a cultural icon after they’ve passed away.” Then he ushers his subject into a softly lit set that looks like an empty planetarium, save for two chairs on a central platform. At the end of forty-five minutes or so of conversation, Falchuk leaves the room, and the subject delivers a final message, facing directly to camera. Fade out, forever.

Nothing on television is quite like “Famous Last Words,” which falls somewhere between “Inside the Actors Studio” and a video will. Falchuk is part Oprah Winfrey, part death doula, part celebrity Grim Reaper. The subject, like Schrödinger’s cat, is both alive and newly deceased. The show’s promise is that, unlike in other interviews, these well-publicized figures can finally speak freely, knowing that it will be seen only after they’re gone. “I’m dead, so I won’t have repercussions,” Goodall notes cheerily. Dane, flashing his handsome-devil eyes, says, “It’s a weird concept to kind of grapple with. You and I are talking here, right now, and we’re both very alive. And, at the same time, when this exists—if it ever does—I won’t be here.” Falchuk told me, “The idea is that, for the first time, these very famous people are going to give a safe interview, where they don’t have to worry about what they say.”

As someone who interviews celebrities for a living, I appreciate any twist to the form, which can get bogged down by promotional pablum and canned anecdotes. We can thank Denmark for the show’s specific innovation: Falchuk and his producing partner, Mikkel Bondesen, who is Danish, adapted “Famous Last Words” from a series created by Mikael Bertelsen, “Det Sidste Ord” (“The Last Word”), which covers subjects who are, in Falchuk’s words, “Danish famous.” They borrowed the basic aesthetics from the Danish version: the cameras are discreet and remotely operated, and the crew have no access to the audio, giving the subject a veil of privacy. The spare set—Falchuk pointed out “the Zen quality of the color of the wood”—is transportable. Goodall’s and Dane’s episodes were filmed in L.A., in a location “tucked away from all the typical stages,” Falchuk said, while Steinem’s took place on the West Side of Manhattan. Once an interview is taped, it’s quickly edited and put in a vault. Only a tiny number of people know who’s on the roster, including just “one or two people at Netflix,” Falchuk told me. “It’s all highly, highly classified, with lots of N.D.A.s.” When a subject dies, the Netflix apparatus leaps into motion. Unlike with its other shows, Netflix posts the new episodes before adding subtitles in other languages, to avoid adding translators into the inner sanctum.

So far, Falchuk has filmed seven episodes, four of which are still under lock and key. The first one was shot more than three years ago and has yet to be seen. Steinem, who sat for her interview in February, 2025, was the fourth to be filmed; Goodall and Dane were fifth and sixth, respectively. I imagined a Whiteboard of Death in the Netflix office, but Falchuk insisted that there’s nothing that ghoulish. Presumably, though, his job is something of a morbid guessing game, like prewriting obituaries. Plenty of luminaries have turned him down. “The majority of people aren’t ready to do it,” he said. He typically asks first for an informal conversation. He met Steinem at her apartment, he recalled, where she sat on her couch and they discussed “things that were important to her” before she agreed. Goodall wanted her interview to cover current affairs—a dicey prospect, since no one knew how much time would elapse before it appeared. (It turned out to be only seven months.) Dane, who died at fifty-three, wanted his two young daughters to know who he was.

Inevitably, each interview turns to mortality itself. Goodall, perhaps surprisingly, says that she believes in an afterlife, while Dane presumes that “when the lights go out, it’s over.” Steinem says that we’re alive whenever someone thinks of us, which is something of a hedge. The conversations take strange turns. Goodall enters in a turtleneck and an Africa-shaped necklace, clutching a stuffed monkey, and downs some whiskey (“for my throat”), then launches into a well-worn story about dung beetles. Midway through, Falchuk asks if she believes in God, and Goodall recalls a monsoon season in Malaysia when she successfully “asked the rain to stop.” When Falchuk asks whom she imagines will greet her in the afterlife, she says that she wants to see her “special” chimps and her childhood dog, plus her mother—but doesn’t much care about her two husbands. She was in love with both men, she explains, but “wasn’t enough in love.” The one man she truly loved, she reveals, was married to someone else. But she declines to give his name, so as not to upset his family. There are repercussions, after all.

Dane’s episode is rawer. Unlike Goodall and Steinem, who lived to their nineties, he has the air of a man robbed by illness. In a wheelchair and struggling to speak (“I sound like a frog,” Dane complains), the onetime Dr. McSteamy from “Grey’s Anatomy” revisits his turbulent past: his father’s apparent suicide, his mother’s “black belt in denial,” his failed marriage, his addiction problems, his history of self-loathing. “It’s kind of a fucked-up way of realizing that you were enough the whole time, when everything gets taken away,” he says. Every so often, he breaks into a mischievous grin, his dreamboat charisma undimmed. And, whereas Goodall addresses her “final message” to all of humanity (“Do your best while you’re still on this beautiful planet Earth”), Dane delivers his directly to his daughters, Billie and Georgia, advising them to live in the moment, fall in love, and choose their friends well. It’s absolutely shattering. As the lights fade and the dates 1972-2026 appear beside his profile, it comes as a shock that he’s dead. His presence on camera—roiled, charming, vulnerable—is so incandescently alive.

Steinem, dressed in a chic lipstick-red longline blazer, is the show’s steeliest subject yet. She enters on Falchuk’s arm, with a cane, and seems skeptical at first, swatting away the host’s suggestions that their conversation is “private” (“Except we’re being recorded!”) and that she’s the “face of the feminist movement.” (Women of color, she says, are central to the cause.) She recounts her oft-recounted life story with poise and self-deprecating humor. But she seems to find all the talk of her own death lightly amusing, and she comes off as much too booked and busy to dwell on her own demise. (Case in point: she was scheduled to appear at our own New Yorker Festival next month.) “I don’t know if we can contemplate our own nonexistence,” Steinem says dryly. The one question that stops her cold is about her late husband’s death: as he was ailing, she recalls, they took a tiny plane to California to see his family. Falchuk asks if she cried during the flight. “No, I was just scared,” she replies. “Crying connotes a solution.”

This has been a late-summer season of mourning: Hayden Panettiere, Dolly Parton, Tim Curry, Yayoi Kusama. The public reckonings with these figures’ legacies—the troubled former child star gone too soon, the beloved icon, the cult favorite, the complicated eccentric—have come in a cascade. Often, when someone close to us dies, we feel a pang of irony: the one person we most want to talk about our grief with is the deceased. The same is true of public figures: Who could have soothed our pain over the loss of Dolly Parton better than Dolly Parton? “Famous Last Words” offers a balm, along with the promise, fulfilled or not, of unguarded honesty. (I do hope that one of its subjects will take the opportunity to settle some scores.)

Falchuk hopes to help society dispel the “taboo of death.” “We are suffering with a culture of a lot of people refusing to face the fact that they’re not going to be here forever, and that they are wonderfully irrelevant,” he told me. Look around at the billionaire biohackers trying to achieve immortality and you see that he has a point. Like a hospice nurse, Falchuk himself has had to get comfortable with mortality. “It’s been a transformative experience, because I’m intentionally bringing death into my life,” he said. The release of each new episode is bittersweet: “I’m still grieving them as people that I care about. It’s weird to think they’re gone.” ♦

title: In “The Sun Never Sets,” Joe Swanberg Strips Romance to Its Bones
author: @NewYorker
content:
Joe Swanberg has a career of remarkable stylistic variety. He started, in 2005, as a do-it-yourself filmmaker, with budgets in the low four figures, and built up an informal stock company of then unfamiliar actors who quickly distinguished themselves in the field—including Greta Gerwig, whose career was launched by her leading role in his freewheeling 2007 movie “Hannah Takes the Stairs.” In 2013, he changed course drastically, directing Anna Kendrick, Olivia Wilde, Jake Johnson, and Ron Livingston in the romantic comedy-drama “Drinking Buddies.” The project was followed by a set of similarly star-powered movies and three seasons of his Netflix series “Easy,” which ran from 2016 to 2019. The release of his new feature, “The Sun Never Sets,” his first in six years, starring Johnson (their fourth film together) and Dakota Fanning, shows the persistence of his distinctive sense of cinematic form and his keen ability to shape elaborate stories from precise ideas. But the film also demonstrates that he has found new ways of working, with new results—he has thrust his ideas to the foreground.

The movie is set in Anchorage, Alaska, where Wendy (Fanning) operates a bulldozer on construction sites. She’s an unmarried woman in a romantic relationship with Jack (Johnson), an apparently fortysomething money manager transplanted from New York and a divorced father of two young children, Abby (Charlie Golike) and Jude (Kincaid Zatalokin). The couple is jovial and tender, independent and connected, and Wendy and the children have developed a warm bond. But there’s a problem: Jack is set in his domestic and paternal ways, and he doesn’t want to get married or have any more children. For Wendy, Jack’s red lines aren’t an issue, but he thinks that Wendy, who’s thirty-one, would eventually regret renouncing marriage and children, so he insists that they take a six-month break in the relationship. He has no doubts about his love for her and no intention of dating other women, but he wants her to date other men so that, by way of comparison, she can assure herself that what she wants from life is life with him, on his terms. What could go wrong?

Surprised and bewildered, Wendy goes on a grudging date with an awkward, doting friend (Brandon Daley) who has long had a crush on her. At the bar with him, she’s startled to make eye contact with an ex-boyfriend named Chuck (Cory Michael Smith), a small-aircraft pilot and a rough-mannered outdoorsman, also around thirty, who has just come back to town. They broke up three years ago, seemingly after some ugliness; now they instantly become a couple again, and Jack desperately tries to undo his agreed-upon plan.

The dramatic mechanism of “The Sun Never Sets” is exquisitely precise—the story’s stakes, in the big picture, are slight, but, for its principals, they’re colossal, catastrophic, life-changing, and Swanberg makes every turn feel like a twist of a knife. What’s especially unusual is how the film makes the underlying structure of this drama visible, rather than making its effects felt in the action. Swanberg displays a seemingly physical awareness of that construction, exposing the story’s large-scale architectural lines as if images were made of glass.

This attention to dramatic framework is a logical extension of Swanberg’s prior body of work. All of his films are largely rooted in improvised performances—he creates stories, plots them out into scenes, and then grants the actors a large margin of freedom in inventing dialogue and stage business. It’s what he did when working with not-yet-professionals and utterly untrained actors in his first films; it’s what he also did with “Drinking Buddies,” “Easy,” and everything in between; and he does it in “The Sun Never Sets,” too. In order to make the method work—which is to say, in order to give the actors guidelines tight enough to shape their performances to a sharp point—he has always made each scene’s function in the plot specific and conspicuous. From there, his casts’ inventive performances push his movies in two directions, bringing a filigree of detail to the story that Swanberg might never have anticipated, and uniting the actors with the characters they play. But “The Sun Never Sets” shifts the balance of these elements and thus gets striking new results from the cast.

“The Sun Never Sets” elides characterization. It rarely suggests what might be happening in the inner lives of its characters; it gives few clues about their interests, tendencies, ideas, or principles, and only grants them those traits which fit the logic of the drama like pegs in slots. The story has no shadows; the characters exist as what they are onscreen, and it’s hard to imagine them off it. This extreme foregrounding of character in terms of action endows the cast with a retrospective air of typecasting, in a positive sense—the actors seem made for their parts, coalescing with their characters temperamentally.

Considered from one angle, the movie is superficial and conventional, zipping heedlessly between the characters without fretting about point of view, creating scenes that don’t so much illuminate characters as simply push the story along. For instance, the film starts with Wendy’s visit to a marina in the hope of buying a particular boat; it quickly turns out to be something of a sticking point with Jack, who’s not an outdoorsman and has no desire to join her time aboard it. In the next scene, at an outdoor gathering, her friend Lindsay (Debby Ryan) announces that she’s pregnant; the elaborate surrounding bustle all but evaporates beside the disclosure that the two friends have long planned to get pregnant around the same time. Wendy laments to Jack that she has lost, as she puts it, her last friend who can join her spontaneously on fun adventures. The fault lines are thus quickly drawn, and the increasing stress prompts Jack to impose, that very night, his strategic pause on the relationship.

In most other films, these narrow constraints would be unequivocal failings. But in “The Sun Never Sets” they’re features, not bugs. The perspective sustained throughout isn’t that of any one character but that of Swanberg himself, and the movie proceeds as if he’s not so much suspensefully turning over its cards one by one but, rather, bringing out, with a dazzling clarity, its conceptual ideal from behind the tangle of events. Swanberg is focussed on his theoretical vision of modern romance—and forgive me for not spoiling it, but the ironies are whiplash-keen and psychologically audacious. The effect is to make the story feel almost like an allegory, abstracting just about everything that it touches—characters, settings, décor, dialogue. It is as if he designed the situation at the center of the movie to show that the traits of its characters are irrelevant to the results.

“The Sun Never Sets” is, so to speak, an experimental film—it looks at its situation as if under a microscope. It’s an extraordinary film masquerading as an ordinary one, a conventional romance on the surface that, on reflection, reveals Swanberg’s philosophical view of love: that people are drawn together by something fundamental, deep in the bedrock of selfhood, that transcends whatever manifest traits they might have in common.

I’m not sure that this idea holds as a general rule. I think that some seemingly surface-level character traits have a direct pipeline to the magma of soul and identity; other traits don’t. One of the most interesting and useful things that romantic drama, classic or modern, can do is to distinguish essential characteristics from trivial ones. Swanberg’s earlier films took such distinctions seriously. For instance, an exemplary scene in “Hannah Takes the Stairs” involves young screenwriters’ criticism of the Bush Administration and their discussion as to whether or not to include it in their work. By contrast, “The Sun Never Sets” exists in an atemporal, ahistorical void. Those early films were among the prime examples of what was then dubbed mumblecore: personal films, raw and free, made with self-conscious attention to performances emerging from real lives and converging with actors’ identities—and ideas.

The reason for these films’ emphasis on the many threads and trends of personality is, above all, youth. The thirteen ultra-low-budget features that Swanberg made between 2005 and 2012 (he was indeed prolific) gave the sense that they emerged from the stuff of his life, from observations within his social circle, reflecting his immediate realm of experience. As befits stories of young outsiders beginning careers and developing their art, they were stories of uncertainty, instability, struggle, and a search for identity itself; every aspect of a character is worthy of representation because much thought goes into the weighing of them all, their hierarchical triage. For the young filmmaker, as for the young person, personalities are tangled woods of curiosity and risk.

“The Sun Never Sets” may be personal in important ways (Swanberg is the divorced father of two children named Jude and Abby). But it also shows that Swanberg—who is twenty years into his career—has come to a clearing, with a strong sense of what he considers the essentials. What’s above all personal in “The Sun Never Sets” is the idea itself, the reflection on love and its strange destinies. The thinning-out of the film is also a clearing-out, putting his standpoint on the action into plain view. In his early films, Swanberg usually did his own cinematography; although his stories were, even then, conceived and shaped with precision, his images—even simple, locked-down tripod shots—were irrepressibly expressive. By contrast, the cinematography of “The Sun Never Sets,” by Eon Mora (who has worked with Swanberg since 2015), is so plain and inexpressive—so open, bright, and blank—that it’s practically a degree zero of pictorial neutrality, a visual correlate for abstract objectivity.

His earlier films offer the immediacy of real-time creation, of something not unfinished but unreworked, thrust onto the screen with an impulsiveness that’s balanced by the careful conception behind it. In “The Sun Never Sets,” the observation has been done in advance, in thought, and the working-out comes off as predetermined and inevitable. That’s why it’s better to have seen “The Sun Never Sets” than to see it, better to think about it than to experience it. The movie is filled with painful events, even laced with a chilly current of pain, along with an ultimate sense of overcoming and healing, however ironic it may be. The film leaves a viewer with authentic consolations and gratifications in the rearview mirror that seemed harder to discern while moving ahead into the unknown with the sun in one’s eyes. ♦

title: Welcome to the Age of AI Crime and Punishment
author: Brendan Fitzgerald
content:
What do privilege and accountability look like for an AI agent on the wrong side of the law? Evan Ratliff rounds up a collection of challenging cases in which AI agents have functioned as co-conspirators in criminal acts, offered courtroom statements on behalf of deceased victims, and perpetrated deeds that, for humans, are considered to be illegal. Legal teams have already sought to seal their clients’ chats with AI agents, likening the exchanges to conversations with an attorney. Ratliff’s feature is an omnibus, and you’ve likely encountered one or two of his stories via other outlets. Here, the concerns he gathers together reveal the breadth of challenges facing the American legal system.

AI chatbots are already serving as confidants and co-conspirators, assisting and even encouraging humans acting on their darkest impulses. They’re occupying ersatz roles as therapists and lawyers, relationships our legal system typically shields with confidential privilege. They’re producing new kinds of criminal evidence and offering up the beguiling possibility of preventing crime before it happens. And as they’re given more autonomy across our digital and physical systems, they’re even gaining the ability to commit crimes themselves, absent specific human instruction — and, perhaps, in defiance of it.

What Happens When a Kid’s Robot Best Friend Dies?

title: The America That 9/11 Made
author: @NewYorker
content:
The America That 9/11 Made

A quarter century after the attacks, the grief, wars, and political furies of their aftermath still shape American life.

September 6, 2026

Photo illustration by Cristiana Couceiro; Source photographs from Getty

I was jammed into an elevator in Minneapolis this summer, heading for the fiftieth floor, up like a shot, when someone tapped my shoulder. I wiggled in place, craned my neck around. “Hey, I know you,” a woman behind me said, smiling. “I took a class with you. I was in your lecture when the planes hit the towers.” We stepped off together—floor fifty turned out to be a wall of windows—and looked out at the city spread vertiginously below us, remembering that moment, twenty-five years ago, in a Boston University lecture hall. The class, The Emerging United States, started at 8 A.M., so early that the student athletes brought breakfast and the room smelled like Egg McMuffins. That morning, we’d been in the eighteen-twenties, and I’d been blathering about Andrew Jackson and the penny press when cellphones across the hall started bleating like lost lambs.

Goddammit, I’d thought. No phones in class. Then someone gasped, and someone shrieked, and someone called out that he’d received a text from his sister in New York, and the towers, oh my God, oh my God, the towers, thousands of people, Jesus no, oh my God. That couldn’t be true. Could it? Plenty of students didn’t have phones then (I didn’t), and texting was spotty. The phones kept ringing, baa baa. The Pentagon? The students were polite, hesitant. “Please, please answer your phones,” I said. “Pick up, call back, call.” The rest of us waited. A student talking to her father said that the planes had come from Logan and he wanted to know, Was she O.K., was Boston under attack? We knew nothing. What was safest: stay or go? Go, I decided. I ended class. Go straight to your dorms, and be safe, be safe. Then I got on my bicycle, turned on a radio bolted to the handlebars, listened to the unfathomable news, looked up at the clearest, bluest sky—no planes, no planes, no planes—and pedalled across the river to a day-care center to pick up my very little boys because mammals gather their young.

Every September 11th, people assemble near Ground Zero for the tolling of a bell, the whispering of prayers, the offering of flowers, the waving of flags. For twenty-four years, the bell has tolled six times: at 8:46 A.M., when a plane crashed into the north tower; 9:03 A.M., when a plane hit the south tower; 9:37 A.M., when a plane hit the Pentagon; 9:59 A.M., when the south tower fell; 10:03 A.M., when Flight 93 crashed into a field in western Pennsylvania; and 10:28 A.M., when the north tower fell. Between bells, mourners read aloud the names of the nearly three thousand people who died that day. There will be a seventh bell-tolling this year, for the thousands who have since died by suicide, or from cancer and other illnesses caused by the ravages of terrorism.

The day’s events are measured in minutes, a ticking clock; the grief in years, a beating heart. “When it began, September 11, 2001, seemed like just another ordinary day,” Mike Kelly writes in “After Ground Zero: Everyday Americans and the Unhealed Scars of 9/11.” Just before 7 a.m., a teen-ager heads to high school; his father goes into the city for a meeting. A young mother dresses her children; her husband begins his commute to Cantor Fitzgerald. A firefighter starts his shift in Queens. A priest dons his robes. A Morgan Stanley assistant vice-president boards a train. By noon, thousands have died, including a two-year-old girl flying to Disneyland, an eighty-five-year-old man travelling to his son’s wedding, and more than four hundred of the first responders who raced to the Twin Towers. Kelly focusses on what followed—“the emotional ruins and brokenness left behind in the lives of ordinary people”—as when, a month later, Kristen Breitweiser was informed that her husband’s left arm had been found, or when, three years later, she was notified that one of his shoulders had been identified, and that, given improved DNA testing, more news would likely follow. How long would this go on? “Would there be a call about Ron’s leg?” she wondered. “His torso? His head?”

Breitweiser has been a prominent voice among family members and survivors who have pressed for a fuller account of 9/11. Their efforts led to the 9/11 Commission Report, published in 2004, which, though riveting and detailed, held no one in the U.S. government responsible for intelligence lapses that failed to stop the hijackings. For many families, the opening of the 9/11 Memorial & Museum, in 2014, brought no solace. Steve Kandell—whose twenty-eight-year-old sister, Shari, was among the more than a thousand people whose remains were never identified—was an early visitor. Later, he wrote about inspecting artifacts and images in the three-hundred-and-fifty-million-dollar, hundred-and-ten-thousand-square-foot museum, from “the husk of an ambulance” to “handwritten pleas for help” and “dusty, ownerless Topsiders encased in glass”:

Everyone should have a museum dedicated to the worst day of their life and be forced to attend it with a bunch of tourists from Denmark. Annotated divorce papers blown up and mounted, interactive exhibits detailing how your mom’s last round of chemo didn’t take, souvenir T-shirts emblazoned with your best friend’s last words before the car crash. And you should have to see for yourself how little your pain matters to a family of five who need to get some food before the kids melt down. Or maybe worse, watch it be co-opted by people who want, for whatever reason, to feel that connection so acutely.

The rubble had been cleared, a report written, a museum built. Artifacts are still being collected: the Smithsonian National Museum of American History is exhibiting severed seat belts from Flight 93, singed I.D. badges from the Pentagon, battered briefcases from the Twin Towers. But there are other kinds of rubble, the dust and debris of anguish and fury.

On the fifteenth anniversary of 9/11, Kristen Breitweiser told Mike Kelly, “I’ve waited fifteen years. My husband was murdered with three thousand people and not one person has been held accountable. How is that possible?”

But has no one been held accountable? Millions have suffered, and hundreds of thousands have died. George W. Bush declared a global war on terror on September 20, 2001; the U.S. went to war in Afghanistan on October 7th. That war, the longest in American history, lasted twenty years. The Iraq War began in 2003. U.S. Special Operations Forces killed Osama bin Laden in 2011. The global war on terror has never been declared over. Brown University’s Costs of War project estimates that post-9/11 American military operations in Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, Yemen, and Pakistan killed nearly a million people between 2001 and 2023, including more than four hundred thousand civilians. Non-civilian deaths include more than seven thousand U.S. service members, more than eight thousand military contractors, more than twelve thousand allied troops, and more than twenty-eight thousand U.S. service members and veterans who have died by suicide.

Janet Reitman weaves together character sketches to reckon with the aftermath of 9/11 in “The Inheritance: An American Tragedy in Five Acts.” After Marlo Cadeddu, an East Dallas lawyer who had once worked on the forty-sixth floor of the north tower, learned of the attack, Reitman writes, “she started to cry and kept on crying for what felt like five years.” She couldn’t stop thinking about how “one of the planes had flown directly into an elevator shaft, severed the cables, and sent cars filled with people plummeting seventy, eighty stories.”

The hijackers were dead. The search for their collaborators and other terrorists in what was now called the homeland proceeded under terms established by the Patriot Act. Many Muslim Americans hid or fled; between 2002 and 2003, thirteen thousand faced deportation proceedings. People around Cadeddu began disappearing: “The Lebanese stock boy at Kroger. The assistant professor of Middle Eastern history. The Palestinian grocer. The Pakistani computer scientist who spent every single night and weekend with his family. Sometimes they’d vanish for a few hours, or a day; other times they’d be gone for good.” Cadeddu became a leading defense attorney for Muslim Americans caught in dragnet sweeps that the F.B.I. was conducting across the country. Her clients included Mufid Abdulqader, whose half brother led Hamas; the F.B.I. arrested Abdulqader in 2004 and charged him with raising millions for terrorists. (Sentenced to twenty years, he was released in 2024.)

Terry Albury joined the F.B.I. as a counterterrorism expert in Minneapolis in 2001. He told Reitman that his training included viewing 9/11 footage over and over: “The planes hitting the towers, the smoke pouring out of the buildings, the people jumping to their deaths, the buildings collapsing into a toxic cloud. Death, destruction, devastation.” It was, he said, “like watching a snuff film.” He knocked on doors and grilled people based on what he considered scant evidence. In 2016, Albury began leaking documents to The Intercept. He was discovered, arrested, charged under the Espionage Act, and sentenced to four years in prison.

Nathan Damigo, a marine, completed two tours in Iraq, returned with P.T.S.D., attempted suicide twice, then committed violent crimes. He needed someone to blame—for the friends he watched die, his pain, everything. In prison, he began reading David Duke:

“Doesn’t it bother you that white people are being replaced by foreigners in our own country?” he asked his brother.

“Actually, man, not really.”

Out of prison, Damigo founded a white-supremacist group. In 2016, after attending the Republican National Convention, in Cleveland, he went to San Francisco and called through a bullhorn, “If you are here illegally, it’s time to go home. America is not your home.” The next year, at the Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville, neo-Nazis carrying tiki torches chanted a slogan of his coinage: “You will not replace us!” Dust and debris, anguish and fury.

In Minneapolis this summer, looking from the fiftieth-floor windows, I thought of how masked federal immigration agents had killed Renée Good and Alex Pretti in this beautiful city, and how the head of the Department of Homeland Security accused them of “domestic terrorism,” digging through the rubble, in vain, for Americans to blame.

A quarter century—a generation—has passed since the towers fell. My little boys are grown men. The students from that lecture hall have children of their own. They live in a different, and even angrier, America.

For years, as a first-day icebreaker, I asked students: What’s the first event of worldwide historical significance that entered your consciousness when you were young? One year, every student said 9/11, and a sophomore said, “My father died in the towers.” The room fell silent. There was no coming back from that answer. I stopped asking the question. ♦

  • Parents disagreed on whether to vaccinate their children. Then the kids got sick.

title: A Mississippi Death Penalty Jury Was Seated. With One Black Juror.
author: Seyward Darby
content:
Earlier this year, the US Supreme Court heard an appeal from death row inmate Terry Pitchford, who was denied relief by the Mississippi Supreme Court after his attorneys claimed Black people were illegally struck from his jury. Investigative reporter Hannah McAlilly delves into the case, and into the wider problem of racial prejudice in the selection of juries in Mississippi:

A prosecutor struck a Black woman for having “red dyed hair” and in another, a prosecutor struck a Black man because he had “a ponytail, a sort of strange hair design.” That prosecutor told the judge he was concerned the juror might identify too closely with the defendant, who also was of a similar age. “Both have unusual hair styles,” the prosecutor said. 

Prosecutors struck Black jurors who, they said, seemed angry, irritated or inattentive. A Black woman was struck because the prosecutor didn’t like her “vibe.” Another, who worked a night shift before showing up to jury selection, was struck for being “fidgety” and looking “angry.” Another was struck because she “frowned a lot.”

title: How Fast You Walk May Determine How Long You Live - Nautilus
content:
You don’t actually need to take 10,000 steps a day to stay fit. That figure comes from the marketing campaign for a Japanese pedometer called the Manpo-Kei, which translates to “10,000 steps meter.” It’s proved to be a remarkably resilient myth, though. 

Featured Video

So how many steps should you take per day? A new study published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine has some answers.

Physical activity researchers from the University of Sydney tracked the steps and walking pace of more than 100,000 middle-aged adults enrolled in the U.K.’s BioBank program for seven consecutive days. They then followed their health for roughly eight years to record any differences in mortality between four separate groups: those who took less than 5,000 steps per day; those who took between 5,000 and 7,500; those who took between 7,500 and 10,000; and the overachievers who averaged more than 10,000 steps. During the study period, nearly 1,700 of the participants passed away, and around 500 of them died of cardiovascular disease. 

Read more: “Here’s Why Our Walking Gets Slower As We Age”

Interestingly, the researchers found several different combinations of steps and pace associated with a reduced risk for premature death. People taking less than 5,000 steps per day saw a substantially reduced risk of mortality, but only if their pace was brisk (80 steps per minute). In fact, people taking these short, quick walks had the same risk of premature death as those who walked between 5,000 and 7,500 steps per day at a slow pace (60 steps per minute).

According to the researchers, the key seems to be walking at a speedy clip for at least half an hour per day. Those who did so showed a progressively reduced risk of death from any cause—at least among the groups walking less than 7,500 steps per day.

But what about the others? 

People walking between 7,500 and 10,000 steps seemed to be the healthiest, with their premature mortality risk reduced the most, even compared to those taking more than 10,000 steps. Per the team, the human body runs into diminishing returns around that mark. 

So, again, there’s no need to take 10,000 steps a day, but you may want to pick up the pace a little when you are out and about.

title: The 17 Minutes That Changed America
author: Krista Stevens
content:
If you make time for one 9/11 anniversary story this year, make it Garrett M. Graff’s piece. This is no mere retrospective. For National Geographic, Graff takes us through that Tuesday morning 25 years ago to explain how America lost its sense of security, minute-by-minute on the morning of September 11, 2001.

It was now 8:53 a.m. There were just 10 minutes left in America as we knew it.

FBI director Robert Mueller was in his first week on the job, sitting in his office suite on the seventh floor of the J. Edgar Hoover Building in Washington. . . .Toward the end of the meeting, someone interrupted to tell Mueller a plane had crashed in New York. Sitting in a briefing on al Qaeda, deep in a conversation about terrorism, Mueller turned and looked out the window at the blue sky beyond and asked, “How could a plane not see the tower? It’s so clear out today.”

Truthfully, terrorism in 2001 just wasn’t something most Americans thought about, outside of the movies or the occasional evening news story or headline. It was a plot device for thrillers, not a perpetual source of anxiety at shopping malls, schools, or public events. And even in the cinema, the “terrorists” were less ideological enemies doing existential battle against the Great Satan and more often the disgruntled genius or vaguely European criminal mastermind. Think Dennis Hopper’s villainous former bomb squad officer in the 1994 blockbuster Speed or Alan Rickman’s turn as the suave, ruthless radical Hans Gruber in Die Hard.

title: Gloria Steinem Gave It All
author: @NewYorker
content:
It is Wednesday, August 12th, almost four weeks after my last visit with Gloria Steinem in New York. I am in Formentera, a small, windswept island off the eastern coast of Spain, revered for its lack of machinery, to watch the solar eclipse. At half past eight in the evening, there is still daylight, in what will turn out to be the hottest August recorded here since 1961. A crowd is starting to form at the beach. Sweat is running down the backs of my legs, and beside me, a small child is digging a hole in the sand—something pointless and therefore extremely important, in the way things done by children often are.

A cloud has stationed itself precisely where the eclipse is meant to be, but the light changes anyway, not quite into night but into something stranger, as though somebody has reached for the dimmer switch on the world, turned it down, and then slowly turned it back up again. A hush passes from person to person until hundreds of us are standing together, looking upward.

The day before, I received a message from Amy, Gloria’s longtime friend, explaining that Gloria had been mostly in bed since I last saw her. I go back and listen to the first interview that Gloria and I did together, at the Emmanuel Centre, in London, almost ten years ago, not long after we first met. We spoke about her memoir “My Life on the Road,” erotica, the political scientist Valerie Hudson, and the problem of gender inequality—its unnerving invisibility, and its enormous scale. Maddeningly, almost everything we talked about is even more relevant today than it was then.

Listening to the interview through my car speaker, I can hear myself trying to figure out, in real time, how the hell she does it: how she is so at ease with herself, so grounded in her opinions without ever becoming rigid, how someone can possess convictions that strong and yet wear them that lightly. Most of all, I am in awe of her authenticity; there appeared to be almost no gap between the woman and what she believed.

The last time I saw her, on July 15th, I had gone to her brownstone, which has served as an organizing and gathering space for activists, writers, and political figures for more than fifty years. The whole place says “history.” The walls are the color of mustard; fabrics and tapestries are everywhere—it is a space that has accumulated rather than acquired its beauty. In the living room, a pair of sirens sits on the wooden mantelpiece. Around the fireplace is a deep-green club fender. Picture frames, plants, and talismans cover all available wall and table space. (For someone who has lived a life of such import, fragments of memory seem surprisingly precious to her.) A small kitchen sits off to one side, and the low ceiling makes the ground floor feel less like a formal living room and more like a club or meeting space. The domestic and the political don’t seem, here, to have been assigned separate rooms.

I remember noticing Gloria’s hands the first time we met, the way her fingernails were carefully shaped and slightly long, a detail of herself she consistently attended to. There was a femininity and a fragility to them that I hadn’t picked up on in photographs. They were always like this when I saw her. Her hair was always in its bob. She was always in black, with a concha belt slung around her waist. That day, she sat in the middle of her low sofa, surrounded by papers and undrunk cups of liquid, looking thinner than she did when I last saw her.

Gloria and I had always talked about marriage and its symbolism—what the institution has meant for women, what we inherit from it, what might be reclaimed or reinvented. Halfway through our conversation, I showed Gloria my own hands, and the ring on my left ring finger, which is meant to represent a different kind of union: a marriage to life itself. I found myself crouched on the floor in front of her, my bare knees on the carpet, explaining the concept, and I felt, very strongly, the sense of something having been passed and shared between us, and I was proud—proud to show her something I had made from ideas we had spent years turning over together.

Eventually, Gloria had to go upstairs for another appointment. Before she disappeared up the spiral staircase, I asked if I could hug her goodbye. As I pressed my body to hers, trying to wrap my arms around her carefully, I knew, with a peculiar certainty, that this would be the last time I saw her.

I have always felt a strange protectiveness toward Gloria, which is absurd when you consider that Gloria Steinem has spent her life protecting the rest of us. She is one of the greatest heroines of the twentieth century.

After the 2016 election, I cried, because I realized that Gloria might die without seeing a woman become President of the United States. There was something unbearable about watching her give almost the whole span of her adult life to democracy, to women, to the stubborn proposition that human beings might organize themselves more fairly, and still never see that particular threshold crossed. I also feared the coming assault on the rights that Gloria had worked so hard to protect.

I remember a male friend telling me that I was overreacting, and that it wasn’t going to be that big of a deal. I stared at the television and said, “They’ll go after Roe v. Wade.” The threat had been stated plainly for years; perhaps what was required was simply the willingness to believe people when they told you what they intended to do.

Gloria somehow held the urgency of it all without ever losing her lightness. When I first began getting to know her, I was anxious: Was I feminist enough, had I read enough, would I pass some imagined female purity test? Gloria gently dismantled the premise. People, she explained, are where they are in their journey of discovery and learning, and feminism had to meet them there. I didn’t have to arrive already knowing everything in order to belong.

Gloria was radical in the original sense of the word, which is derived from the Latin radix, meaning “root”—going to the system underneath the problem rather than attempting to remedy its surface effects—and she somehow held that radicalism alongside an almost unreasonable kindness. I have tried to carry that forward—to hold myself to account while understanding that patriarchy is not something women stand conveniently outside of. We were born inside it; it lives inside us. It has shaped our ideas of beauty, love, goodness, success, and safety, and we cannot simply announce ourselves liberated and be done with it. We can only begin to rectify something after we recognize it; we can only shed a skin once we have outgrown it.

Before leaving Gloria’s brownstone, I had given her a card I had bought in New York, made by the artist Olga Prinku, depicting a glittery silver snake. On the day of the eclipse, I look up what the snake means: transformation, rebirth, healing, knowledge—and feminine power. What a complicated creature we chose for this symbol. I think of the lion, that familiar emblem of masculine power, with his soft, beige fur and magnificent mane, made harmless enough in miniature that little boys sleep with him tucked under their arms. Women get the snake: close to the ground, frightening, blamed for the fall of man, and periodically required to split its own skin open in order to grow.

Gloria seemed to know the same thing about people, that change involves a certain kind of splitting. She could be radical without requiring everyone to arrive at the same revelation at the same moment, and held that generosity alongside an increasingly radical article of faith—her belief in democracy, even as so many of its believers began to wonder whether the whole experiment had failed.

Her papers at Smith College now occupy a hundred and six feet of shelf space. There are very few people I have met about whom I can say, with certainty, that they gave the whole thing, not merely the public bit but the private Tuesdays, too—the days when nobody was watching, when the work was fashionable and when it wasn’t, when there was hope and when hope itself must have required considerable imagination.

When I try to think of the small, funny details that could cut the sadness of writing this—the sorts of things these pieces need—I come up strangely empty-handed. I never ate a burrito with Gloria. We worked together. We talked politics. We talked about books; she gave me books, so many that I sheepishly had to ask her for a tote bag, too, in order to carry them all.

As the eclipse passes, I think about how quiet I have been for quite some time now, and I realize that something about that has to change, because if Gloria is leaving us, then some of us are going to have to get louder. It feels less like a decision than like a law of physics: I think of gravity, of black holes, of the way one body continues to exert a force on another across apparently empty space. I feel Gloria’s gravity still, pulling me toward the horizon and toward a world she could already envision.

She did not get to see it.

Perhaps I won’t either. But this may be the difficult truth about progress that Gloria understood better than most of us: you may spend your whole life walking toward a world you will never enter, but that does not relieve you of the obligation to walk.

The snake does not repair its old skin. The snake outgrows it, pressing itself against the earth, against rock, against whatever will give it enough resistance to begin the challenging work of leaving one form behind. In Formentera, I watch the moon move through shadow and back toward the light, and, for a moment, it seems as if the whole world is changing its skin. ♦

title: Court Grants TRO Barring "Threatening, Intimidating, and Retaliation Action ... Without a Legitimate Law Enforcement Purpose" Against ICE Watcher
content:
From Judge Michael Newman (S.D. Ohio) Friday in Moorman v. Doe No. 1; since this is a decision at the temporary restraining order stage, the factual assertions are preliminary conclusions by the judge, not final findings of fact:

Plaintiff Sean Moorman … alleges Defendants—seven unidentified United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement ("ICE") officers, in their official capacities—have retaliated (and continue to retaliate) against him for engaging in activity protected by the First Amendment ….

The motion for TRO was filed around 7 P.M. on Tuesday, September 1, 2026. The Court heard extensive oral argument the next day at 4 P.M., lasting more than one hour…. At the time of the phone conference, the AUSA [who represented the government -EV] failed to contradict the Moorman's factual assertions and requested a two-week extension to file a response brief. As detailed herein, based on the serious nature of the allegations involved, and the threat of ongoing constitutional violations, this extension would be inappropriate. See Elrod v. Burns (1976) ("The loss of First Amendment freedoms, for even minimal periods of time, unquestionably constitutes irreparable injury.")….

Moorman volunteers as an "ICE watcher" in his spare time. As uncontradicted by the AUSA, Moorman "lawfully and peacefully" documents interactions between ICE officers and the Springfield community, noting potentially violent or unlawful action by ICE officers….

According to Moorman, by August 20, 2026, certain ICE officers had identified Moorman as an ICE watcher and began "lashing out" at him.  Specifically, on August 20, 2026, Moorman recorded … [an] ICE vehicle driven by Defendant John Doe No. 2…. "John Doe No. 2 turned his Jeep around and accelerated dangerously towards [Moorman]'s vehicle as though to ram it, before veering away at the last moment and disappearing."

The next morning, on August 21, 2026, Moorman stood on the side of a main road in Springfield alongside a reporter wearing a press badge, and recorded ICE officers conducting an arrest. An ICE officer wearing a yellow vest, identified as Defendant John Doe No. 1, approached Moorman and the reporter, put his phone in their faces as if to scan or take a picture, and then continued walking.

Later that day, Moorman entered the parking lot of a Cracker Barrel restaurant in Springfield to observe and photograph ICE officers after identifying [other] known ICE vehicles…. Upon seeing Moorman enter the parking lot, the ICE officers, who had just exited their vehicles, immediately re-entered their vehicles. Moorman observed Defendant John Doe No. 1 looking at him with binoculars.

The ICE officers then pulled out of their parking spots. As Moorman proceeded to exit the parking lot, the ICE officers "looped around and followed [him]." With the ICE officers following him, Moorman circled around the Cracker Barrel, another adjacent parking lot, and an adjacent dead-end road.

After a few minutes, Moorman and the ICE officers returned to the Cracker Barrel parking lot. Each time Moorman pulled into a parking spot, the ICE officers would pull in front of and block Moorman's vehicle and prevent him from moving out of his spot. The ICE officers would each block Moorman's vehicle for ten seconds at a time, sometimes taking photos of his license plate, before allowing him to move to another location in the parking lot. This happened for the next ten to fifteen minutes. Throughout this encounter, Moorman put his vehicle into park each time the ICE officers were in front of him and kept his hands on the steering wheel so that the officers could see them.

Moorman eventually was able to exit the Cracker Barrel parking lot but ended up on a dead-end road nearby. At that point, Moorman was approached by the Nissan Pathfinder driven by Defendant John Doe No. 3, who was masked and wearing large sunglasses. The officer waved at Moorman, apparently signaling Moorman to follow him; Moorman complied with the officer's direction.

As Moorman followed the Nissan Pathfinder, a Hyundai Sante Fe driven by Defendant John Doe No. 1, followed behind Moorman. The ICE officers led Moorman toward a rural area on the outskirts of Springfield where Moorman and his wife live. During oral argument, the AUSA offered no explanation for the ICE officers' leading Moorman back to his residence.

Upon realizing this, Moorman called other volunteer ICE watchers to warn them about the situation. He also called his wife, who was home alone with their pets, and told her that ICE officers were heading toward their home, and to lock the doors and stay inside. Moorman's wife cowered in the house holding a baseball bat out of fear.

The Nissan Pathfinder then pulled up to the end of Moorman's driveway and slowed. Defendant John Doe No. 3 put his arm out of the vehicle's window and pointed at Moorman's house. He took pictures of Moorman and his wife's vehicles. After this encounter, Moorman and his wife installed a security camera at their home and now keep their doors locked at all times.

ICE officers continued to engage with Moorman throughout the next several days. [Further details omitted for space reasons. -EV] …

The Court takes notice that national incidents similar to those described herein have devolved into circumstances leading to serious injury or loss of life to officers and members of the community alike….

Moorman seeks a TRO enjoining Defendants, and those acting in concert with them, from "taking further threatening, intimidating, and retaliatory action against [him] in response to his exercise of his First Amendment rights … without a legitimate law enforcement purpose." According to Moorman, such actions include, but are not limited to, pursuing his vehicle, attempting to box in his vehicle, approaching him, traveling to his home, or shouting at him to intimidate him, without a legitimate law enforcement purpose. While these events considered seriatim would be less concerning, when considering the allegations together, they amount to a substantial and troubling violation of Moorman's First Amendment rights….

First, Moorman engaged, and continues to engage, in protected conduct. Eight circuits have expressly held that filming government agents performing official duties in public is protected under the First Amendment. Other courts in this district have also recognized this right….

While some courts have imposed reasonable time, place, and manner restrictions on an individual's right to record law enforcement, the record shows that Moorman conducts his ICE watching activities in a safe and lawful manner; he records ICE activity only while in public spaces, takes precautions to make sure he is not threatening officers' safety such as keeping his hands visible, follows applicable traffic laws, and does not interfere with ICE's enforcement operations. Moorman has also participated in specific training for individuals who wish to monitor law enforcement activity in a safe, lawful, and peaceful manner.

Second, Moorman has suffered adverse action(s). An adverse action is one that "would deter a person of ordinary firmness from continuing to engage in" protected conduct under the First Amendment….

While some retaliatory acts are so de minimis that "they do not rise to the level of being constitutional violations," Defendants' actions in this case surpass that threshold…. Moorman asserts that Defendants, over the course of several days, nearly swerved into his vehicle; scouted Moorman's home for no legitimate purpose (on multiple occasions) causing Moorman's wife to fear for her safety; continuously stalked Moorman around Springfield; and cut off and trapped Moorman's vehicle in a parking lot. At minimum, ICE officers seized Moorman in the Cracker Barrel parking lot on August 21, 2026, see U.S. v. See (6th Cir. 2009) (noting that blocking a person's car with a patrol car was a warrantless seizure), thus constituting adverse action. See Wood v. Eubanks (6th Cir. 2022) (holding that a Fourth Amendment seizure amounts to an adverse action for the purpose of a First Amendment retaliation claim).

Finally, Moorman has demonstrated a causal connection between his protected conduct and the adverse actions allegedly perpetrated by Defendants…. Defendants remain free at a later stage to show that they would have taken the same action regardless of Moorman's protected conduct. However, at this time, nothing in the record supports that showing, and Moorman need only demonstrate a likelihood of success, not a certainty.

Here, Defendants cannot identify a single, legitimate basis for continuing to harass and intimidate Moorman for exercising his First Amendment rights. Defendants, and others acting in concert with them, including all other ICE officers stationed in Springfield, Ohio, will suffer no cognizable harm from a TRO that does no more than require them to comply with the Constitution they are already bound, and have sworn, to follow. Moreover, it is always in the public interest to enjoin unconstitutional conduct.

Moorman's proposed TRO is limited in scope; it requests that Defendants refrain from harassing and committing retaliatory acts—including pursuing his vehicle, approaching him, photographing him in a threatening manner, traveling to his home, or shouting at him for the purposes of intimidation—without a legitimate law enforcement purpose.

To that end, two items merit mention. First, the Court is not telling ICE— part of the executive branch—how to do its job.

Second, the Court is not entering into the political fray to suggest whether or not ICE should be engaging in deportation activities in Springfield, Ohio.

What the Court is holding is that, when government actors engage in such conduct, the Constitution requires that it be undertaken without hazing, retaliation, or harassment, particularly with regard to an individual who does not interfere with ICE's enforcement function or police power. As Justice [Gorsuch] aptly said, the "Government is not free to disregard the First Amendment in times of crisis." Roman Catholic v. Diocese of Brooklyn v. Cuomo (2020) (Gorsuch, J.) (concurring) ….

David J. Carey, Freda J. Levenson, and Carlen Zhang-D'Souza (ACLU of Ohio) represent plaintiff.
